newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian race MP greeted by protests.
newsitem.headline: Australian race MP greeted by protests.

text.p: Supporters and opponents of Australia's race row politician Pauline Hanson clashed noisily in the southern city of Adelaide on Wednesday as protesters barricaded the entrance to the launch of her One Nation party.

Scuffles broke out as members of the extreme right group National Action, who later accused police of failing to protect their right to attend a public meeting, pushed through the crowd of about 600 protesters to attend the suburban launch.

Protesters held banners declaring "Migrants in, Racists out" and "Pauline peddles poison" as about 700 people arrived to hear the independent politician who has split the nation with her views on immigration, multiculturalism and Aboriginal welfare.
Media reports said thousands of people attended a candlelight vigil in Adelaide's city centre, also protesting against Hanson.
With a backdrop proclaiming "Pauline the Patriot," the populist mother-of-four from conservative Queensland state urged supporters to vote for her at the next election, due in 1999.
Even before its official registration as a party, One Nation has gained around 10 percent support in opinion polls, and Hanson says she wants to capture the balance of power in the next election.

Hanson told the audience that Australia was no longer the place they had been born in, and repeated earlier calls for a freeze on immigration, cuts in funding to multiculturalism, and the deportation of immigrants convicted of serious crime.
Welcomed with a thunderous standing ovation and later mobbed for autographs, Hanson denied being a racist, saying: "Criticism is not racism, patriotism is not racism."
One supporter said he welcomed her views: "I am prepared to share my country with anybody, but I do not want them to change it into their country".

"Things are no good in Australia now, we kow-tow to other people who come in here now," said a disappointed elderly woman, turned away from the suburban wedding venue, which had earlier tried to cancel Hanson's booking after threats of violence.

Another elderly woman protesting against Hanson's views said the former chip-shop owner was seeking a return to the White Australia immigration policy of previous decades, when black and Asian migrants were excluded.
"I sincerely hope she never gets the balance of power because there is going to be a lot of trouble then. She is already destroying the name of Australia overseas," she said.
